summary: On Thursday, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn won Tennessee's Republican gubernatorial primary, defeating U.S. Rep. John Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts, The Associated Press projected.
The race marks Tennessee's first open gubernatorial contest since 2018, as Gov. Bill Lee is term-limited and cannot seek a third consecutive term.
Blackburn campaigned on supporting President Donald Trump's "America First Agenda," aiming "to make Tennessee America's conservative leader," while Rose emphasized he is "not a career politician."
Memphis City Council member Jerri Green secured the Democratic nomination, setting up a Nov. 3 general election matchup against Blackburn in the heavily Republican state.
Republicans have dominated Tennessee in recent years, with Trump carrying the state in 2024 by nearly 30 points over Kamala Harris, positioning Blackburn as the heavy favorite.
title: Source Icon

summary: President Donald Trump signed two executive orders aimed at limiting the scope of birthright citizenship and directing federal agencies to crack down on the commercial "birth tourism" industry, reviving a key immigration policy objective despite previous legal setbacks.

One order seeks to deny automatic U.S. citizenship in certain cases involving children born to parents who allegedly entered or remained in the country through fraudulent use of temporary visas, with the administration arguing that the policy fits within constitutional exceptions.

The second order instructs the Departments of State and Homeland Security to develop measures targeting birth tourism operations in the United States and abroad, as federal scrutiny of companies offering such services continues.

Legal experts expect the new directives to face immediate court challenges, following the U.S. Supreme Court's June 2026 ruling that struck down Trump's earlier executive order restricting birthright citizenship under the Fourteenth Amendment.
title: Trump signs executive orders targeting birthright citizenship

McConnell has not announced when he will return to the Senate but continues to engage with staff on Senate business while recovering at home.

summary: The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination more than 100 times during a hearing on the federal COVID-19 response.

Committee Chairman Rand Paul announced plans to send the contempt referral directly to the Department of Justice for potential prosecution, bypassing a full Senate floor vote where the measure would likely fail to clear a 60-vote threshold.

Republicans contend that Fauci cannot claim Fifth Amendment protections, arguing that his pre-emptive presidential pardon from Joe Biden eliminates federal criminal liability for his pandemic-era conduct.

Fauci and panel Democrats strongly rejected the resolution, with Fauci stating he invoked his constitutional rights because Paul's explicit objective was to force testimony that could be used to fulfill public pledges to put him "behind bars".

The action creates a novel legal test for congressional oversight, forcing the Justice Department to evaluate whether a presidential pardon strips a witness of self-incrimination privileges or if remaining risks—such as state-level prosecutions or perjury charges—validate constitutional protections.
title: Senate committee votes to hold Fauci in contempt for refusing to answer COVID questions

summary: The Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz as director of the Atlanta-based CDC in a 51-44 vote on Wednesday, making her the agency's 22nd leader and first Senate-confirmed director in nearly a year.

Turmoil has gripped the CDC since Republican President Donald Trump returned to office last year, with the agency losing more than 3,000 employees—over one-quarter of its workforce—amid layoffs and resignations.
Schwartz is the third Trump nominee for CDC director in the past 18 months; earlier, the Senate canceled a hearing for David Weldon, and Susan Monarez was ousted less than a month after confirmation.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., initially questioned whether Schwartz would resist pressure from health secretary Robert Kennedy, but gained confidence after further discussions, overcoming gridlock in the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.

With medical and law degrees plus Coast Guard leadership experience, Schwartz faces the challenge of stabilizing the agency amid depleted morale and ongoing political friction within federal health leadership.
title: New CDC director is confirmed, giving agency its first permanent leader in a year

Republican officials redrew the 5th District this year, expanding it from central Tennessee into Memphis with 82% new voters, significantly complicating reelection for Ogles, a conservative Freedom Caucus member.

Ogles faced scrutiny after the FBI seized his cellphone in 2024 during a campaign finance investigation, though the Justice Department recently abandoned the probe. Hatcher campaigned as a pro-Trump alternative emphasizing his farming background.

Republicans chose state Sen. Brent Taylor for the 9th District, while state Rep. Johnny Garrett won the 6th District primary after Rep. John Rose decided to run for governor. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn secured the GOP nomination to succeed Gov. Bill Lee.

A State Department spokesperson said "online presence vetting" ensures visa eligibility, adding that "Officers use a variety of methods to make informed decisions that protect national security, prevent fraud and ensure a thorough review of applicants."

The administration has previously revoked visas for foreign nationals over comments about the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and for students engaged in pro-Palestinian activism, signaling a pattern of visa status use.

Following last month's Department of Homeland Security rule changes tightening journalist duration limits, the unclear implementation timeline for this new social media policy leaves foreign journalists uncertain about their future status in the United States.
title: US to vet social media of foreign journalists applying for visas, report says

summary: On Thursday, Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger announced she is formally intervening in the proposed $67 billion merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy, marking the first time a Virginia governor has taken such action before the State Corporation Commission.

Governor Ghazala Hashmi warned that regulatory guidelines written in 1940 are ill-equipped for modern utility mergers, while Spanberger aims to ensure the deal prioritizes affordable bills, workforce protection, and clean energy investment.

Dominion Energy CEO Bob Blue and NextEra Energy CEO John Ketchum defend the merger, citing $1.8 billion in bill credits and an 18-month job protection guarantee, with Blue calling it a "transformational opportunity" to serve millions across four states.

The State Corporation Commission has 180 days to review the application, though some lawmakers are urging a special legislative session to extend the timeline and ensure critical questions about the merger are thoroughly answered.

Dominion and NextEra expect the transaction to close in the second half of 2027, while Clean Virginia Executive Director Brennan Gilmore warns that such consolidation could lead to higher costs for Virginia consumers.
title: Gov. Spanberger to Intervene in NextEra Energy and Dominion Merger

Boeing updated its manufacturing processes to address the cracking issue on newly built airplanes, reflecting the manufacturer's effort to resolve quality control problems identified in the production line.

The FAA did not ground the fleet, as the directive requires usage-based inspections and repairs before affected aircraft return to service, providing multiple opportunities to detect cracks before structural integrity is compromised.
This scrutiny follows intense oversight since an Alaska Airlines door plug blew out in January 2024, when the National Transportation Safety Board found four missing bolts during delivery.

Last month, regulators proposed a separate airworthiness directive requiring inspections of seat assemblies on 453 Boeing Max jets to verify proper installation, reflecting broader quality control challenges.
title: FAA Orders Inspection of Hundreds of 737 Max Jets for Cracks

Tennessee Republicans redrew congressional lines in May, breaking up the Memphis metro area and eliminating the state's only majority-minority district, shifting the political landscape where Pearson has voiced strong opposition.

Internal instability plagues the Conservative caucus, which has seen six other members exit since the 2025 election. These departures include four floor-crossings, Saskatchewan MP Cathay Wagantall's resignation, and Quebec MP Richard Martel's appointment to the Senate.

Winning 52 percent of the vote in 2021, Brock captured the riding, though a June shuffle removed him as justice critic. The district remains listed as "leaning" Conservative on the poll aggregator 338Canada.ca.

Despite reports of his impending departure, Brock affirmed "full support" for Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre , calling him the "leader Canada needs." This stance contrasts with growing scrutiny over party direction and public spats within the conservative movement.

Any upcoming by-election in the district will serve as a critical barometer for Conservative popularity in the region. Poilievre visited the riding earlier this week amid broader concerns over party direction, declining fundraising, and a restive caucus.

summary: On Thursday, the Justice Department accused Duke Law School of unlawfully considering race in admissions, marking the latest Trump administration action targeting higher education institutions for alleged discrimination.

Investigators found Duke Law intentionally discriminated in 2023, 2024, and 2025 classes, violating the Civil Rights Act and the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard.

Reviewers used tags to identify race-correlated traits, giving Black and Hispanic applicants roughly 3.5 times higher admission probability than equally qualified Asian applicants, according to findings.
Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said the DOJ is seeking a voluntary settlement with the university, though the department will file suit if compliance efforts fail.

Recent actions also targeted medical schools at Yale University and the University of California, Los Angeles, as the department continues monitoring institutions for compliance with federal nondiscrimination laws.
title: Justice Department Says Duke Law School Illegally Considered Race in Admissions

summary: On Friday, barrister Gabrielle Bashir cross-examined the complainant in the Sydney Local Court trial regarding inconsistencies in his account of alleged sexual assaults by Alan Jones , who has pleaded not guilty to 22 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching.

The complainant, now in his 40s, alleges Jones assaulted him on nine occasions during 2003 and 2004 at the broadcaster's Fitzroy Falls property; Jones denies all charges involving six alleged victims across Sydney and the NSW Southern Highlands.

Bashir repeatedly suggested the athlete fabricated allegations based on media reports, arguing, "You're giving different accounts because this is a fabricated allegation against Mr. Jones." The defense cited inconsistencies including testimony about a robe and tennis match after alleged assaults.

Defending his testimony, the athlete insisted, "No, it's based on what he said on the night," after Judge Glenn Walsh lifted a suppression order late Thursday, enabling publication of cross-examination answers during the complainant's fifth day of questioning.

This marathon hearing spans incidents between 2003 and 2020 involving six alleged victims across Sydney and the NSW Southern Highlands, as the court continues examining historical claims while Jones maintains his innocence regarding all 22 charges.
title: Athlete Changes Jones Abuse Evidence but Denies Lying

summary: On Wednesday, the Toronto International Film Festival unveiled its 2026 Docs program, featuring 21 titles from 20 countries, including Alex Gibney's nearly four-hour investigative documentary Musk and opening-night selection Rapinoe.

TIFF also selected Avi Nesher's Our Loves, which deals with characters caught in the October 7 massacre, for its Centerpiece section; producers view the selection as countering an unofficial international boycott of Israeli cinema.

Liron Edery, United King Films head of marketing and distribution, stated the boycott is "gradually crumbling" and that the film provides a platform for the "Israeli story" and narratives of "repair, healing, and change."

TIFF documentary programmer Thom Powers defended the festival's programming decisions, noting that legal challenges against The Bibi Files were dismissed in court, expressing confidence in rigorous vetting of high-profile documentaries.

The 2026 program includes Maiken Baird's Edward Said: Between Worlds, an intellectual biography of the Palestinian-born activist; this selection demonstrates TIFF's commitment to showcasing intellectual narratives alongside contemporary social justice stories.
title: TIFF Selects Avi Nesher’s Oct. 7 Drama for Centrepiece World Premiere

summary: On Thursday, President Donald Trump signed a proclamation imposing 15% tariffs on imported polysilicon and related derivatives, citing national security concerns over United States reliance on foreign supplies.

Invoking Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, the administration seeks to protect domestic manufacturers from Chinese competition; Chinese companies became the world's dominant polysilicon producer by the last decade.

The Commerce Department will oversee minimum import prices of $21 per kilogram for polysilicon and $100 for ingots, while Trump's order authorizes incentive programs for firms investing in domestic factories.
Shares of First Solar Inc. climbed 8% and T1 Energy Inc. rose 6.3% following the announcement, though manufacturers warned the December 4 implementation date could spur stockpiling of cheap imports.

Jon Toomey, president of the Coalition for a Prosperous America, called the directive a strategy to reshore industry as the United States seeks to nurture a solar supply chain dormant for over a decade.
title: Trump Orders 15% Tariffs, Price Floors on Polysilicon Imports

summary: Senator Bernie Sanders said he does not plan to endorse Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, citing unfamiliarity with the race and a general lack of involvement in many governor races.
Francesca Hong is a member of the Democratic Socialist of America and is a frontrunner in the August primary.
Hong has faced criticism for her progressive and socialist positions, including controversial statements, which may impact her appeal to centrist and rural Wisconsin voters in the general election.

Sanders's decision not to endorse Hong has sparked criticism, with commentators noting his past endorsements of other controversial progressive candidates and questioning his doubts about her electability.
title: Sanders doesn’t believe he will endorse Hong: ‘I don’t think so’

summary: An internal Fisheries Department memo released Thursday warned that legislation backed by President Donald Trump threatens North Atlantic right whale survival by delaying federal protections until 2035.
The bill, introduced by Democratic representative Jared Golden of Maine, would delay protections by nearly a decade to allow time for industry-friendly measures with fewer implications for fishing.

Fewer than 400 of these endangered whales remain, with roughly 70 breeding females, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration; warming waters and ocean traffic force them into deadly collision zones.

The bill cleared the House Natural Resources Committee last month and could reach the Republican-controlled Congress this summer, where it is likely to pass and potentially require Canadian harvesters to reduce impacts on the species.

Beyond Golden's proposal, NOAA is considering changing ship-speed rules in place since 2008, which Amy Knowlton of the New England Aquarium described as "a disaster," while the White House confirmed Trump's advisers would recommend signing the bill.
title: Whale species’ survival jeopardized by bill backed by Donald Trump: internal memo

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the ruling as accountability for a “youth mental health crisis,” leaning on charged phrases like “knowingly harmed” and “concealed” to portray Meta as deliberately endangering children, while right-leaning coverage casts it as a hard legal blow, stressing “JUST IN,” “court forces,” and “major setback” alongside the scale of “$567 million.” The sharpest dividing line is whether the story is about corporate wrongdoing or judicial overreach; center pieces sit between them, emphasizing the “public nuisance” finding and youth-safety remedies.
Both sides agree Meta must pay and appeal, but they diverge on whether the case signals remedy or reckoning.
summary: On Thursday, Chief District Court Judge Bryan Biedscheid of the New Mexico First Judicial District Court ordered Meta to pay $567m and implement strict safety measures for teenage users on Facebook and Instagram.
This ruling follows a two-phase trial brought by New Mexico Attorney General Torrez, where a jury previously fined Meta $375 million for 75,000 violations of the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act.

To address the youth mental health crisis, the court mandated a 90-hour monthly usage cap for users under 18 and required Meta to hide like counts and prohibit unconnected adults from messaging minors.
The $567m fund will support treatment, awareness, and prevention services over a five-year period, with $420 million specifically allocated for youth mental health treatment.
While Judge Biedscheid labeled Meta a "public nuisance" akin to pollution, federal law limits the court's ability to enforce age-verification tools on children under 13.
title: Meta ordered to pay $567 million in New Mexico for teen mental health fund

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the settlement through harm and accountability, stressing “deadly,” “yearslong legal battle,” and even the “3 people” killed and property damage, while right-leaning coverage stays narrower, spotlighting the $106 million as the key resolution and keeping the broader fallout de-emphasized.
The center adds the most legal context, noting “nearly seven years after” the collapse, the grand jury’s no-indictment decision, and related lawsuits.

The main dividing line is whether the story is a tragedy needing redress or a court ending a dispute; both sides agree on the collapse’s seriousness and the settlement, reflecting shared concern over a disastrous construction failure.
summary: On Thursday, Orleans Parish Civil District Court Judge Kern Reese approved a $106 million settlement ending a yearslong legal battle over the 2019 Hard Rock Hotel collapse in New Orleans.

The 18-story hotel project partially collapsed in 2019 during construction, killing three workers—Jose Arreola, Quinnyon Wimberly, and Anthony Magrette—and damaging nearby property along Canal Street.
Lawsuits from 490 plaintiffs, including injured workers and businesses, were consolidated into one case against 21 defendants, according to lead counsel Mark Glago.
A special master will eventually distribute the settlement funds to claimants, Glago noted, with specific disbursement details expected later.

Although a grand jury previously declined to indict anyone following the tragedy, this court-approved settlement formally resolves the yearslong civil litigation surrounding the New Orleans hotel collapse.
title: Judge Approves $106 Million Settlement over Deadly 2019 Hard Rock Hotel Collapse in New Orleans

summary: On Thursday, China's embassy in Buenos Aires accused the United States of hypocrisy after Argentine electricity cooperative CALF alleged U.S. officials threatened to revoke executives' visas for partnering with Huawei.

President Javier Milei maintains a close alliance with President Donald Trump while deepening commercial ties with China, as the U.S. administration increasingly invokes a modern-day Monroe Doctrine to counter regional influence.

CALF alleged executives received WhatsApp messages warning of visa restrictions, prompting the Argentine Federation of Electricity and Public Services Cooperatives to defend its members and request institutional dialogue.

China's embassy stated U.S. actions reflect "arrogance and prejudice" and urged Washington to end its "hegemonic practices," even as Argentina renewed its bilateral currency swap agreement with China on Wednesday for five years.

Finance Secretary Pablo Quirno plans to visit China in the coming months to strengthen commercial ties, supported by significant Chinese investment including more than 20 automakers selling over 60 models in Argentina.
title: China's embassy in Argentina accuses US of obstructing cooperation

summary: On August 2, investigators discovered an unknown substance around the bases of 16 trees at Burnt Cedar Beach in Incline Village. The Washoe County Sheriff called the deliberate destruction "deeply troubling" for the community.

Authorities have investigated similar cases at Burnt Cedar Beach since 2022, with nearly 30 trees targeted over the last four years. Deputies previously found substances poured around bases or drilled into roots.

Capt. Joseph Colacurcio of the Washoe County Sheriff said damage could exceed $300,000 if the mature trees die. Investigators collected soil samples matching previous incidents to identify the substance.
Sheriff Darin Balaam said on Monday that officials are seeking public assistance to identify the responsible party. Anyone with information regarding case number 26-4225 should contact 775-328-3001.

Investigators believe the perpetrator could face criminal charges under Nevada law for intentionally destroying vegetation. While Burnt Cedar Beach remains open, authorities continue searching for evidence to hold the responsible person accountable.
title: Trees intentionally poisoned on Lake Tahoe beach, officials say

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds the civil-rights arc, stressing the end of “segregation monitoring” and pairing it with the board’s upbeat language about “freedom” and the “best interest” of the community; right-leaning coverage is thinner and more restrained, treating the same move as simply the end of “61 years” of federal “oversight,” a framing that hints at skepticism toward long federal supervision.
The sharpest dividing line is whether the story is about racial-redress legacy or about local control after Washington steps back.
Center coverage adds the most context, noting the Justice Department “reversed course” under Trump.
summary: On Thursday, Bossier Parish Schools and the Justice Department agreed to end 61 years of federal desegregation oversight, concluding the long-standing legal monitoring near Shreveport on the first day of classes.

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill announced the settlement, arguing these decades-old cases are 'expensive, ineffective' and infringe upon local control, following her work with the Concordia Parish School Board last month.
Because the parents who filed the original 1964 lawsuit are deceased and their children could not be contacted, the oversight order proceeded with dismissal.

Bossier Schools Superintendent Jason Rowland said the dismissal grants 'freedom to make our own decisions,' while the district collaborated with the Justice Department for decades on infrastructure changes.

The Justice Department reversed course under Trump, with officials framing segregation orders as 'federal intrusion,' while Louisiana officials describe these mandates as relics from when Black students were forbidden from schools.
title: Louisiana school board and federal government end 61 years of segregation monitoring
